title: Ratios, unit rates and rates of change
blurb: Split amounts in a ratio, tell part-to-part from part-to-whole, find unit rates and average speeds, and read a rate of change.
question: In a nursing cohort of 63 students, the ratio of women to men is 7:2. An IV of 1,000 mL runs over 8 hours. A patient's temperature falls from 101.6°F to 99.2°F in 6 hours. The TEAS asks how many men there are, the rate in mL per hour, and the rate of change. How do you handle each one?

teach.body: Formally, a ratio compares two quantities by division and can be written a:b, a to b, or a/b. A rate is a ratio of quantities with DIFFERENT units, such as miles per hour or mL per hour, and a unit rate is the amount for exactly one unit. In plain English: a ratio says 'for every 3 of these, there are 2 of those'; a rate says 'this much for each one of that'. In both, the order of the words decides the order of the numbers.

teach.h: Boys to girls is 3:2 in a class of 35
teach.caption: To use a part-to-part ratio on a total, add the parts first: one part = 35 ÷ 5 = 7.

teach.h: Worked example: sharing in a ratio
items: Split $500 in the ratio 2:3:5. Add the parts: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts.
Simplify ratios like fractions: 12:18 = 2:3 (divide both by 6).

teach.text: A 3:2 ratio does NOT mean 3/2 or 60% of anything by itself. With boys to girls 3:2, boys are 3/5 (60%) of the class and girls are 2/5 (40%). And order matters: 'girls to boys' is 2:3, the reverse of 3:2.

teach.h: Unit rate: divide by the 'per' quantity
teach.body: To find a unit rate, divide the first quantity by the amount of the unit after 'per'. $4.50 for 3 lb: 4.50 ÷ 3 = $1.50 per lb. 150 miles in 2.5 hours: 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 miles per hour. To compare deals, find each unit price in the same unit; the lower unit price is the better buy. If your rate comes out as hours per mile when the question wants miles per hour, you divided the wrong way.

teach.h: Which gauze pack is the better buy?

teach.caption: The biggest pack is not always the cheapest per item. Divide each time.

teach.h: Average speed for a whole trip

items: An IV of 1,000 mL is ordered over 8 hours. Rate = 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL per hour. Check: 125 × 8 = 1,000. ✓
A nurse counts 18 heartbeats in 15 seconds. A minute has 4 sets of 15 seconds, so 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.
Check the heart rate as a unit rate: 18 ÷ 15 = 1.2 beats per second, and 1.2 × 60 = 72. ✓
Always label the units: mL per hour and beats per minute, never just '125' or '72'.

teach.caption: 68°F at 9 a.m. to 80°F at 1 p.m.: (80 − 68) ÷ (13 − 9) = 12 ÷ 4 = 3°F per hour. A constant rate makes a straight line.

teach.h: Rate of change from two points
items: Rate of change = change in output ÷ change in input = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁).
A child is 40 in tall at age 4 and 46 in tall at age 7. Change in height: 46 − 40 = 6 in. Change in age: 7 − 4 = 3 years.
If the output goes down, the rate is negative: 101.6°F to 99.2°F in 6 hours is −2.4 ÷ 6 = −0.4°F per hour.
Order matters: a:b means a first. Add the parts to use a ratio on a total.
Unit rate = amount ÷ number of 'per' units. Lower unit price = better buy.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, never the average of the speeds.
Rate of change = change in y ÷ change in x, with units and a sign.

summary: You can now share an amount in a two- or three-part ratio, convert part-to-part ratios to fractions of the whole, find unit rates and better buys, and compute an average speed for a whole trip. You can also calculate a rate of change from two data points, including negative rates.

A.q: In a nursing cohort of 63 students, the ratio of women to men is 7:2. How many of the students are men?
A.why: Total parts: 7 + 2 = 9. One part: 63 ÷ 9 = 7. Men: 2 × 7 = 14. Check: 49 women + 14 men = 63, and 49:14 = 7:2. ✓

whyNot.0: 18 treats the ratio as a fraction of the whole (2/7 × 63); men are 2/9 of the cohort.
whyNot.3: 9 divides 63 by 7 instead of by the 9 total parts.

A.q: Which package of exam gloves has the lowest price per glove?

whyNot.0: $0.0849 per glove is the highest of the four.
whyNot.1: $0.082 per glove is close, but higher than the 250-pack's $0.07996.
whyNot.2: The biggest box works out to $0.083 per glove, more than the 250-pack.

A.q: An IV bag of 1.5 L is to run over 12 hours. What is the rate in milliliters per hour?

whyNot.0: 0.125 divides 1.5 by 12 without converting liters to milliliters; it is 0.125 L/h.
whyNot.1: 8 divides time by volume (12 ÷ 1.5), which inverts the rate.

B.q: Devon drives 90 miles to a clinical site at 60 mph and returns the same way at 45 mph. What is his average speed for the round trip? Round to the nearest tenth.
B.why: Time out: 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5 h. Time back: 90 ÷ 45 = 2 h. Total: 180 miles in 3.5 h. 180 ÷ 3.5 = 51.43, about 51.4 mph.

whyNot.0: 52.5 mph averages the two speeds. He spends longer at 45 mph, so the true average is lower.
whyNot.2: 105 mph adds the two speeds together.
whyNot.3: 25.7 mph divides one-way distance (90) by the total time.

B.q: A patient's temperature was 101.6°F at 0800 and 99.2°F at 1400. What was the average rate of change?
B.why: Change: 99.2 − 101.6 = −2.4°F. Time: 0800 to 1400 is 6 hours. Rate: −2.4 ÷ 6 = −0.4°F per hour.

whyNot.1: −2.4°F is the total change over 6 hours, not the change per hour.
whyNot.2: The temperature fell, so the rate of change is negative.
whyNot.3: −2.5 divides the hours by the degrees (6 ÷ 2.4), giving hours per degree.

B.q: A cleaning solution mixes bleach, detergent and water in the ratio 1:3:16. How many milliliters of detergent are in 4 L of solution?

whyNot.0: 200 mL is one part, the amount of bleach.
whyNot.1: 750 mL uses 3/16 of 4,000, comparing detergent with water instead of with the whole.

C.q: On a hospital unit the ratio of RNs to LPNs is 5:3, and there are 24 LPNs. Six more RNs are hired. What is the new ratio of RNs to LPNs, in lowest terms?
C.why: One part = 24 ÷ 3 = 8, so there are 5 × 8 = 40 RNs. After hiring: 46 RNs to 24 LPNs. 46:24 simplifies to 23:12 (divide by 2).

whyNot.1: 4:3 adds the 6 new staff to the LPNs (40:30) instead of the RNs.
whyNot.2: 11:9 adds 6 to each number in the ratio. Ratios change by recounting, not by adding to the ratio terms.
whyNot.3: 23:15 adds 6 to both counts (46:30); only the RNs increased.

C.q: A home-care agency charges $280 for 4 visits and $430 for 7 visits, at a constant rate per visit plus a fixed fee. What is the charge for each additional visit?
C.why: Rate of change = (430 − 280) ÷ (7 − 4) = 150 ÷ 3 = 50 dollars per visit.

whyNot.0: $70.00 is 280 ÷ 4, which mixes the fixed fee into the per-visit charge.
whyNot.1: $61.43 is 430 ÷ 7, the same mistake for the second bill.
whyNot.3: $150.00 is the change in cost for 3 extra visits, not for one.

C.q: In a patient survey, the ratio of patients who rated their care 'excellent' to those who did not is 7:3. What percent of patients rated their care 'excellent'?

whyNot.0: 233.3% treats 7:3 as 7/3; a part-to-part ratio must be turned into part-to-whole first.
whyNot.2: 42.9% is 3/7, comparing the two groups with each other in reverse.
whyNot.3: 30% is the share who did NOT rate their care excellent.

reteach.title: Lemonade by the scoop
reteach.question: A lemonade recipe uses 2 scoops of powder for every 5 cups of water. How does thinking in 'batches' solve every ratio question?

blocks.body: One batch is 2 scoops + 5 cups = 7 units. Any amount of this lemonade is just some number of batches. For 840 units in total, you need 840 ÷ 7 = 120 batches, so 2 × 120 = 240 scoops and 5 × 120 = 600 cups. A rate is a batch of size one: if 3 lb of apples cost $4.50, a 'batch' of 1 lb costs $1.50.

blocks.text: The batch size is the SUM of the parts. Dividing the total by just one part (840 ÷ 5) mixes up part-to-part and part-to-whole.

explain.body: A ratio like 2:5 compares two parts. To find a share of a total, add the parts (2 + 5 = 7), divide the total by that sum, then multiply by the part you want.

items.label: saline as a fraction of the mix
water as a fraction of the mix

test.q: Saline and sterile water are mixed in the ratio 2:5 to make 840 mL. How much saline is in the mixture?
test.why: Total parts: 2 + 5 = 7. One part: 840 ÷ 7 = 120 mL. Saline: 2 × 120 = 240 mL. Check: 240 + 600 = 840. ✓

whyNot.0: 336 mL uses 2/5 of 840, treating the part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole.
whyNot.1: 120 mL is one part, not the 2 parts of saline.
whyNot.3: 600 mL is the sterile water (5 parts).

explain.body: Divide price by quantity to get the price for one unit, then compare like with like.

test.q: A 12-ounce bottle of hand sanitizer costs $4.20 and a 32-ounce bottle costs $10.24. How much less per ounce does the larger bottle cost?

whyNot.1: $0.32 is the larger bottle's unit price, not the difference.
whyNot.2: $6.04 is the difference in total price, not in price per ounce.
whyNot.3: $0.35 is the smaller bottle's unit price.

explain.body: Speed = distance ÷ time. Convert minutes to hours first (1 h 30 min = 1.5 h). For a whole trip, divide total distance by total time.

test.q: A cyclist rides 18 miles in 1 hour 30 minutes. What is her average speed?
test.why: 1 hour 30 minutes = 1.5 hours. 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12 miles per hour. Check: 12 × 1.5 = 18. ✓

whyNot.0: 13.8 reads 1 hour 30 minutes as 1.3 hours. Thirty minutes is half an hour, 0.5.
whyNot.1: 27 multiplies distance by time instead of dividing.
whyNot.2: 0.08 divides time by distance (1.5 ÷ 18), giving hours per mile.

explain.body: Rate of change = change in output ÷ change in input. Keep the units: pounds per month, degrees per hour.

test.q: A toddler weighs 32 lb at 24 months and 38 lb at 36 months. What is the average rate of change in weight?
test.why: Change in weight: 38 − 32 = 6 lb. Change in age: 36 − 24 = 12 months. Rate: 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 lb per month.

whyNot.0: 2 divides months by pounds (12 ÷ 6), inverting the rate.
whyNot.2: 6 lb is the total gain over 12 months, not the gain per month.
whyNot.3: 1.06 divides 38 by 36, using single values instead of changes.
